newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU mulls extending worker consultation rules.
newsitem.headline: EU mulls extending worker consultation rules.

text.p: The European Commission said on Monday it planned to ask employers and unions to negotiate rules requiring single-country companies in the European Union to set up procedures for consulting their workers.
The initiative would complement an EU law that already obliges multinational companies to set up "works councils" or other systems for informing and consulting employees about important developments.

Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn intends to present the new plan to a meeting of EU social affairs ministers on Tuesday in Brussels, Commission spokeswoman Barbara Nolan told a news briefing.
The ministers are also set to formally adopt hard-fought legislation guaranteeing workers who are posted across borders by their employees the same pay and working conditions as those hired locally.
They provisionally agreed the text last June and were waiting for approval from the European Parliament before final adoption.
Flynn will propose that an accord on worker consultation at national companies be negotiated under the EU's Social Protocol, from which Britain has an opt out.
He decided to act after getting positive feedback from most EU states on the need for a European initiative in this area, Nolan said.

At the same time, the Commission has been unable to break a longstanding deadlock between EU states over a related proposal to allow firms to set up as "European companies" and will propose that it be referred to a group of experts, she said.

The European Company Statute -- along with proposals for a European association, European cooperative society and European mutual society -- has been blocked for many years by a dispute between EU states over provisions on worker participation.
Germany has fought to apply its own system of "co-determination" for workers, while Britain wants no mandatory rules.

But Commission proposals for breaking the impasse have met with some resistance, especially from Germany, because they would apply general EU rules on worker "consultation" -- rather than "participation" -- to the new entities.

EU member states -- who are coming under increasing pressure from industry to allow companies to set up under EU rather than national law -- generally support the idea of referring the question to a group of high-level experts, EU officials said.
EU trade unions and employers have negotiated one accord under the Social Protocol so far, covering parental and family leave, which was then turned into EU law.
